syntaxCards.note: Min-heap pops the smallest element. Java and C++ compare with greater<int>() and greater<>(). Python heapq is always a min-heap; use negative values for a max-heap.

snippets.python:
import heapq
heapq.heappush(pq, v)   # min-heap
heapq.heappop(pq)    # smallest
# max-heap: push -v, pop, negate

syntaxCards.note: Two pointers need a monotone invariant: if the sum is too small, left must move right; if too large, right must move left. Sorting first is what makes the monotone step valid.
Prefer the lower-bound half-open form. It has no off-by-one branch and returns the first index where the predicate holds.
BFS with a Queue visits in wave order, so the first time you reach a node is its shortest distance. DFS with recursion or a Stack is for reachability and cycle structure, not distance.
Variable-width windows: add the entering element, then shrink while the window is invalid. The shrink condition must reference the same predicate you tested to expand.
When you need to know whether a value was seen before, a HashMap costs O(1) average instead of a Set scan. Reserve capacity when the input size is known to avoid rehashing.
Write the state definition as a sentence before any code. Tabulation fills a table bottom-up; memoisation recurses top-down. Both compute the same states.
A stack gives O(1) push and pop and surfaces the most recent unmatched opener. Use an ArrayDeque in Java rather than a legacy Stack so insertion order is well defined.

snippets.python:
st = []
st.append(c)
o = st.pop()
empty = not st

syntaxCards.note: The choose-recurse-undo cycle is the whole algorithm. Push before recursing and always pop after, in the reverse order of the push, or sibling branches inherit corrupted state.

Recursion mirrors the tree shape. Preorder visits node then children, inorder is required for sorted binary trees, postorder computes values that depend on both subtrees. Depth can exceed the stack limit on skewed trees, so an explicit stack is safer in interviews.

snippets.python:
def preorder(node, out):
    if node is None: return
    out.append(node.val)
    preorder(node.left, out)
    preorder(node.right, out)

syntaxCards.note: x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit, which yields a running count of set bits. For a power of two, x & (x - 1) is zero.

snippets.python:
x = n
count = 0
while x:
    x &= x - 1
    count += 1
is_pow2 = n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0

syntaxCards.note: For merge problems sort by start time. For sweep problems such as meeting rooms, sort by start and compare each start against a max-heap of end times.
A greedy choice must be locally safe, so it needs a proof: usually an exchange argument showing the greedy pick can be substituted into an optimal solution without loss.
There is no index, so every operation needs a saved pointer. When you remove or reverse a node, capture next before you overwrite it.

snippets.python:
prev, cur = None, head
while cur:
    cur.next, prev, cur = prev, cur, cur.next
return prev

syntaxCards.note: Sum without the plus operator is XOR plus carry. The carry comes from AND, shifted one place left. Keep adding the carry until it is zero.

snippets.python:
MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF
s = (a ^ b) & MASK
carry = ((a & b) << 1) & MASK
while carry:
    s = (s ^ carry) & MASK
    carry = ((s & carry) << 1) & MASK
return s - (1 << 32) if s >> 31 else s

syntaxCards.note: The expensive part of string work is almost always creating a new string. Build into a StringBuilder or a char array and write once at the end, rather than concatenating in a loop.
Reserve capacity when you know the input size. It avoids rehashing, and in Java it is the difference between a map that rehashes on every insert and one that does not.

snippets.python:
from collections import defaultdict, Counter

freq = defaultdict(list)
for i, c in enumerate(s):
    freq[c].append(i)

# counting only:
counts = Counter(s)

syntaxCards.note: Java's Arrays.sort for primitives is a dual-pivot quicksort; for objects it is a tim sort, because you asked for stability by using a comparator. C++ std::sort is introsort: quicksort that falls back to heapsort on bad pivots, so it is never quadratic. std::stable_sort is mergesort and needs O(n) extra memory.

snippets.java:
Arrays.sort(arr);                    // primitives: dual-pivot quicksort
arr.sort((a, b) -> a - b);   // objects: tim sort, stable
Arrays.sort(arr, 2, 6);                // range only
snippets.python:
nums.sort()                 # in place, tim sort, stable
sorted(nums)                # returns a new list
sorted(nums, key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
snippets.cpp:
#include <algorithm>
std::sort(a.begin(), a.end());              // introsort
std::stable_sort(a.begin(), a.end());     // mergesort, needs O(n) memory
std::sort(a.begin(), a.end(), greater<int>());  // descending

syntaxCards.note: Every backtracking problem is the same three lines: choose, recurse, undo. The undo has to happen in the reverse order of the choose, or the next sibling branch inherits a corrupted state and you chase ghosts.

Each node holds a fixed-size array indexed by character value, so lookup is a single array index per character rather than a hash of the whole prefix. Reserve 26 children when the input is known to be lowercase letters.

The whole structure follows from one invariant: everything left is smaller, everything right is larger. Inorder traversal of a BST is therefore sorted, which is the property most BST problems are really asking you to exploit.

Binary search on the answer is the reusable shape: the predicate is monotonic, so you search the answer space instead of the data. Keep the predicate in its own function; that separation is the whole technique.

Integers overflow silently in C and Java. If a result can exceed 2^31 minus 1, promote before multiplying: cast one operand to long. Python integers do not overflow, which is why the same bug can hide there.

snippets.python:
# no overflow, but watch the loop
while b:
    a, b = b, a % b

# modular inverse: pow(x, -1, m)
inv = pow(a, -1, m)

syntaxCards.note: A Fenwick tree is a flat array plus a lowbit walk, so it is the cheapest range structure to implement. A segment tree costs four times the memory but gives an associative combine. If you only need sums and prefix queries, start with Fenwick.

problems.title: Two Sum
problems.statement: Given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. Each input has exactly one solution and you may not use the same element twice.
problems.keyIdea: Trade a nested scan for a remembered past. Store each value with its index as you go, so the complement of the current value is a single lookup rather than a full search.

ladder.label: Brute force
ladder.why: Check every pair. Correct and obvious, but you scan the rest of the array once per element.

ladder.label: Sorted two pointers
ladder.why: Sorting makes the sum monotone in each cursor, so one pointer can be discarded per step. Sorting dominates the cost.

code.python:
s = sorted(nums)
l, r = 0, len(s) - 1
while l < r:
    if s[l] + s[r] == target: return [l, r]
    if s[l] + s[r] < target: l += 1
    else: r -= 1

ladder.label: Hash map single pass
ladder.why: One pass, no sorting. You pay O(n) space to buy back the O(n log n) sort and the second scan.

hints: You need the complement of the current value. What structure makes finding it O(1)?
As you scan left to right, store each value together with its index.
Before storing nums[i], check whether target - nums[i] is already stored. That ordering is what prevents reusing one element.
A HashMap of value to index. One pass over the array.
Pseudocode: for each i, look up need in seen; if found return [seen[need], i]; else seen[nums[i]] = i.

problems.title: Palindrome Number
problems.statement: Given an integer x, return true if x is a palindrome, and false otherwise. A palindrome reads the same backwards as forwards.
problems.keyIdea: Reversing only half the digits is enough. If you keep dividing by ten and stop at the midpoint, the reversed half equals the remaining front half exactly when the number is a palindrome, and you never build the reversed copy.

ladder.label: Reverse the whole number
ladder.why: Convert to a string and compare with its reverse, which is the shortest correct answer. It needs a string allocation, and it is the approach that hides the overflow trap: a reversed integer can exceed the int range for large inputs.

code.python:
s = str(x)
return s == s[::-1]

ladder.label: Reverse the digits arithmetically
ladder.why: Keep halving a copy of the number and building a reversed copy, no strings involved. The trap is that the reversed value can exceed int range, which is why the copy is promoted to long.

code.python:
if x < 0 or (x % 10 == 0 and x != 0):
    return False
rev, half = 0, x // 2
while half:
    rev = rev * 10 + half % 10
    half //= 10
return rev == x // 100 or rev == x % 1000 // 10

ladder.label: Reverse only the trailing half
ladder.why: A palindrome is symmetric, so only half the digits matter. Reversing just the trailing half halves the number of loop iterations and, more importantly, guarantees the reversed value stays within half the digits so overflow cannot occur.

code.python:
if x < 0 or (x % 10 == 0 and x != 0):
    return False
rev, half = 0, x // 2
while half:
    rev = rev * 10 + half % 10
    half //= 10
return rev == x // 100 or rev == x % 1000 // 10

hints: Do you need to reverse all the digits to check symmetry?
No. Only half of them. If the second half reversed equals the first half, the number is symmetric.
What happens to a number ending in zero?
A palindrome cannot end in zero unless it is zero itself, because a leading zero is not representable. Reject those immediately.
Pseudocode: reject negatives and multiples of ten. Take x divided by two, repeatedly take its last digit into an accumulator, and compare the result against the leading half.

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.statement: Given a string containing just the characters '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']', determine if the input string is valid. An input string is valid if open brackets are closed by the same type of bracket and in the correct order.
problems.keyIdea: Nesting is strictly last-in-first-out, which is exactly what a stack guarantees. Push openers, and every closer must match the most recent unmatched opener.

ladder.label: Rescan on every mismatch
ladder.why: On finding a mismatch, restart validation from the beginning. Correct but re-checks the same prefix repeatedly.

ladder.label: Counting brackets
ladder.why: Counts total openings against closings. It detects a missing or extra bracket but silently accepts '{]}' because the ordering is never checked.

code.python:
opening = sum(s.count(c) for c in '({[')
closing = sum(s.count(c) for c in ')}]')
return opening == closing

ladder.label: Stack with type matching
ladder.why: Push every opener, then require each closer to match the stack top. Ordering becomes structurally enforced rather than counted.

hints: Which data structure matches strict nesting order exactly?
Openers must close in reverse order of opening. That is the definition of a stack.
Push openers. On a closer, the stack top must be its partner, or the string is invalid.
A stack of characters, plus a map from closer to opener.
Pseudocode: push '(' '{' '['; for any closer, if stack empty return false, else pop and compare to its partner; at the end return stack.isEmpty().

problems.title: Climbing Stairs
problems.statement: You are climbing a staircase with n steps. You can either climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many distinct ways can you climb to the top?
problems.keyIdea: The ways to reach step i are the ways to reach i-1 plus the ways to reach i-2, because the last move was either one or two steps. That recurrence is Fibonacci.

ladder.label: Tree of all move sequences
ladder.why: Enumerate every possible sequence of 1s and 2s. Exponential because the same subproblem recurs exponentially often.

ladder.label: Memoised recursion
ladder.why: Caching each computed value collapses the exponential recursion into a linear chain. Memoisation with recursion is the top-down form.

ladder.label: Tabulation with two variables
ladder.why: Only the previous two states are ever read, so the whole table collapses to two variables. Same linear time, constant memory.

hints: How many moves reach the final step, and who could have arrived there?
You can only arrive on step i from step i-1 with a one-step move or from step i-2 with a two-step move. Those two cases are disjoint.
Write ways(i) = ways(i-1) + ways(i-2) and then ask how many distinct states exist.
There are n states. A naive recursion recomputes the same states exponentially many times.
Either cache each value (top-down) or fill the values in order from step 1 (bottom-up). Note that only the last two are ever needed.

problems.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
problems.statement: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth. The maximum depth is the number of nodes along the longest path from the root down to a leaf.
problems.keyIdea: The depth of a node is one more than the deeper of its two subtrees. That single recurrence is the entire problem; every approach is just a different way of walking it.

ladder.label: Level order with a queue
ladder.why: Walk the tree one level at a time and count the levels. Simple and immune to recursion limits, but a wide tree holds an entire level in memory at once.

ladder.label: Recursive depth of the taller side
ladder.why: One plus the deeper child is the whole recurrence. It reads as three lines and costs one stack frame per level.

code.java:
if (root == null) return 0;
return 1 + Math.max(depth(root.left), depth(root.right));

ladder.label: Iterative DFS with an explicit stack
ladder.why: Same recurrence, but the depth is tracked explicitly instead of living in the call stack. A skewed tree of a hundred thousand nodes will not overflow.

hints: How do you get from the two subtree depths to the depth of their parent?
The path through a node goes through whichever child is deeper. The other child is irrelevant to the answer.
Try writing the answer as one plus the maximum of two recursive calls.
What is the depth of an empty tree? That gives you the base case.
Pseudocode: if node is empty return 0, else return 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)).

problems.title: Valid Palindrome
problems.statement: Given a string s, return true if s is a palindrome when read backwards, ignoring alphanumeric characters and treating uppercase and lowercase letters as the same. Only alphanumeric characters count.
problems.keyIdea: A palindrome is a symmetric property, so you only ever need to compare mirrored positions. Skip anything that is not a letter or digit and never allocate a cleaned copy of the string.

ladder.label: Clean the string, then reverse a copy
ladder.why: Build the filtered lowercase string, reverse a second copy of it, and compare. Readable and correct, but it materialises two extra n sized strings to answer a question that can be answered in place.

code.python:
clean = ''.join(c.lower() for c in s if c.isalnum())
return clean == clean[::-1]

ladder.label: Two pointers over the original
ladder.why: Same linear scan, but two cursors walk inward from the ends and skip non-alphanumerics in place. No allocation at all, which turns three string allocations into nothing.

code.python:
l, r = 0, len(s) - 1
while l < r:
    while l < r and not s[l].isalnum(): l += 1
    while l < r and not s[r].isalnum(): r -= 1
    if s[l].lower() != s[r].lower():
        return False
    l += 1; r -= 1
return True

ladder.label: Inward scan without inner skip loops
ladder.why: Identical asymptotics to the two pointer version, so this is not a complexity win. The gain is that each cursor advances exactly once per comparison instead of running its own nested skip loop, which keeps the branch predictor happy on long non-alphanumeric runs.

hints: Do you need to build a cleaned copy of the string to compare it?
A palindrome is symmetric, so position i must match position length minus 1 minus i. You can walk both at once.
What do you do with characters that are not letters or digits?
Skip them. Keep one pointer on each end and move each inward past anything that is not alphanumeric.
Pseudocode: l and r start at the ends. Advance past non-alphanumerics, then compare lowercase s[l] with lowercase s[r], then step both inward.

problems.title: Number of 1 Bits
problems.statement: Write a function that takes an unsigned integer n and returns the number of set bits it has, also called the population count. Assume n is a non-negative 32-bit integer.
problems.keyIdea: x AND (x minus 1) clears the lowest set bit in a single operation. Counting how many times you can do that before the number reaches zero is exactly counting the set bits.

ladder.label: Convert to binary and count characters
ladder.why: Write the number out in base two and count the ones. Understandable, but it allocates a string to answer a question about a fixed 32 bit word.

code.java: return (int) Integer.toBinaryString(n).chars().filter(c -> c == '1').count();
code.python: return bin(n).count('1')

ladder.label: Kernighan's trick
ladder.why: Each x AND (x minus 1) removes exactly one set bit, so the loop runs once per set bit rather than once per bit. No allocation, and it skips every zero position.

code.python:
count = 0
while n:
    n &= n - 1
    count += 1
return count

ladder.label: SWAR popcount with fixed masks
ladder.why: Add, subtract and mask in fixed width steps so each operation accounts for two bits, then four, then eight, then sixteen at once. The count takes a handful of arithmetic steps regardless of the input.

hints: How do you remove exactly one set bit from a number in a single operation?
Subtracting one flips the lowest set bit to zero and everything below it to one. AND with that result keeps only the cleared bit.
If you AND a number with itself minus one, what happens to the number of set bits?
It loses exactly one set bit. So loop that operation and count how many times you can before reaching zero.
Pseudocode: while n is not zero, set n = n AND (n - 1) and increment the counter.

problems.title: Reverse Linked List
problems.statement: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list and return its new head.
problems.keyIdea: Reversing is the same local pointer swap repeated along the whole list. Keep one pointer to the part already reversed so nothing is lost on the way.

ladder.label: Copy through an array
ladder.why: Read every node into an array, reverse the array, then build a second list from it. Correct, but it allocates two extra n sized structures and never touches the original pointers.

code.python:
vals = []
cur = head
while cur:
    vals.append(cur.val)
    cur = cur.next

dummy = ListNode(0)
for v in reversed(vals):
    dummy.next = ListNode(v, dummy.next)
return dummy.next

ladder.label: Recursive reversal
ladder.why: The recursion stack holds the rest of the list for you, so the code reads as three lines. It costs one stack frame per node, so a list longer than the stack limit will overflow.

code.python:
def reverse(head):
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return head
    new_head = reverse(head.next)
    head.next.next = head
    head.next = None
    return new_head

ladder.label: Iterative three pointers
ladder.why: The same pointer surgery with no recursion, so the stack never grows with the list. Three pointers and the reversal is done in a single pass.

code.python:
prev, cur = None, head
while cur:
    cur.next, prev, cur = prev, cur, cur.next
return prev

hints: What single pointer change reverses a two node list?
Reversal is local: if a points to b, you want b to point back to a. Each node needs exactly one rewire.
You need a pointer to the node you already reversed, so the next iteration does not lose the finished part.
Keep prev (already reversed), cur (current node) and next (saved before the overwrite).
Pseudocode: while cur: save next, set cur.next to prev, advance prev to cur, advance cur to next. Return prev.

problems.title: Search in a Binary Search Tree
problems.statement: Given the root node of a binary search tree and a target integer, return the node where the target is found, or null if it is not present. A BST has the property that all values in the left subtree are smaller and all values in the right subtree are larger.
problems.keyIdea: The ordering invariant tells you which side can possibly contain the target, so you never visit the other subtree. That halves the search space at every step.

ladder.label: Recursive search of both subtrees
ladder.why: Walk both subtrees looking for the value. It works, and it makes no use of the BST property, so on a balanced tree it visits nodes a logarithmic search would have skipped.

ladder.label: Recursive, use the ordering invariant
ladder.why: Only recurse into the subtree that can hold the target. The tree height h bounds the work, which on a balanced tree is logarithmic.

ladder.label: Iterative descent
ladder.why: The same halving, but as a loop with one cursor, so no stack frames are pushed. Removes the recursion depth limit, which is the only reason to prefer this over the recursive form.

code.python:
cur = root
while cur:
    if val == cur.val: return cur
    if val < cur.val: cur = cur.left
    else: cur = cur.right
return None

hints: What does the BST invariant tell you about which subtree can contain a value smaller than the root?
Only the left one. So the right subtree can be skipped entirely rather than searched and found wanting.
Compare the target against the current node, then which direction do you move?
Left when the target is smaller, right when it is larger, and stop when they are equal.
Pseudocode: while the node exists, if it matches return it, otherwise step left or right according to the comparison.

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.statement: Given a string s, return the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
problems.keyIdea: The window must stay duplicate-free. When a repeat appears, advance the left edge past the previous occurrence rather than restarting the scan.

ladder.label: Check every substring
ladder.why: Enumerate all O(n^2) substrings and verify each with an O(n) set. Quadratic start times linear work.

ladder.label: Sliding window with a set
ladder.why: The outer scan is now linear, but shrinking one character at a time and re-checking the whole window stays quadratic.

code.python:
best = 0; l = 0; seen = set()
for r, ch in enumerate(s):
    while ch in seen:
        seen.remove(s[l]); l += 1
    seen.add(ch)
    best = max(best, r - l + 1)
return best

ladder.label: Sliding window with last-seen map
ladder.why: Remember where each character last appeared. The left edge jumps straight to one past that index instead of creeping forward one character at a time.

hints: What invariant must hold for the current window?
The window can never contain a duplicate. When adding a character that already exists inside it, the left edge must move.
Do not shrink one character at a time. Jump the left edge directly past the previous occurrence of the repeating character.
A map from character to its last seen index. On a repeat, set left to lastSeen[c] + 1.
Pseudocode: for each r, if last[s[r]] >= l then l = last[s[r]] + 1; last[s[r]] = r; best = max(best, r - l + 1).

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.statement: An array sorted in ascending order is rotated at an unknown pivot. Given the rotated array and an integer target, return the index of target if it exists, or -1 if it is not in the array. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity.
problems.keyIdea: At every split one half is still fully sorted. Identify which half by comparing the midpoint against the low bound, then discard the half that cannot contain the target.

ladder.label: Linear scan
ladder.why: Rotation does not affect membership testing. Ignores the sorted structure entirely and fails the stated complexity requirement.

ladder.label: Binary search then linear wrap
ladder.why: Binary search one monotonic run, then scan the tail. Correct and simple, but the scan makes worst-case behaviour unpredictable.

code.python:
l, r = 0, len(nums) - 1
while l <= r:
    m = (l + r) // 2
    if nums[m] == target: return m
    if nums[m] > target: r = m - 1
    else: l = m + 1
return next((i for i, v in enumerate(nums) if v == target), -1)

ladder.label: Modified binary search
ladder.why: At least one half around the midpoint is sorted. Test that half's range against the target and discard the other, halving the window every step.

code.python:
l, r = 0, len(nums) - 1
while l <= r:
    m = (l + r) // 2
    if nums[m] == target: return m
    if nums[l] <= nums[m]:
        if nums[l] <= target < nums[m]: r = m - 1
        else: l = m + 1
    else:
        if nums[m] < target <= nums[r]: l = m + 1
        else: r = m - 1
return -1

hints: Why does ordinary binary search break on a rotated array?
Because the array is not globally sorted, the usual discard rule is no longer trustworthy. You need a different signal each step.
At any midpoint, one of the two halves is still sorted. Determine which one by comparing nums[left] to nums[mid].
If the left half is sorted, the target is either inside it or in the right half. If the right half is sorted, the opposite applies.
Pseudocode: if nums[l] <= nums[m] then range-check the left half, else range-check the right half. Narrow one bound each iteration.

problems.title: Permutations
problems.statement: Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible permutations. You can return the answer in any order.
problems.keyIdea: Build the answer one position at a time. Choose an unused value for the current slot, recurse, then undo the choice so the next branch starts from the same state.

ladder.label: Enumerate all orderings
ladder.why: Generate every arrangement directly. The factorial growth is the problem to be solved, not worked around.

ladder.label: Used-array bookkeeping
ladder.why: Same factorial cost but tracks used values explicitly, which makes the logic portable to problems with duplicate elements.

code.python:
used = [False] * len(nums)
cur = []
def bt():
    if len(cur) == len(nums):
        out.append(cur[:]); return
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        if used[i]: continue
        used[i] = True; cur.append(nums[i])
        bt()
        cur.pop(); used[i] = False
bt()

ladder.label: Swap into position, no used array
ladder.why: There is no asymptotic win left, because n! permutations must be materialised. The gain is allocation: this version reuses the input as the working state, so the extra memory is the recursion stack instead of a separate used array plus a fresh list per leaf.

hints: What does one branch of the search tree represent?
A partial arrangement. A complete leaf is a full permutation. You need to grow the branch and then restore it.
At each level, try every value not yet used, recurse, then remove it.
The critical detail is undoing the choice. Without the undo, every sibling sees a corrupted array.
Pseudocode: if the current path is full, record it. Otherwise for each unused value: push it, recurse, pop it.

problems.title: Group Anagrams
problems.statement: Given an array of strings strs, group the anagrams together. You can return the answer in any order.
problems.keyIdea: Two words are anagrams exactly when they contain the same characters with the same counts, so the sorted word is a perfect dictionary key. Or a 26 wide count vector, which skips the sort.

ladder.label: Sort each word and compare every pair
ladder.why: For every pair, sort both words and check equality. Quadratic in the number of words and it re-sorts the same word once per comparison.

ladder.label: Sorted word as a map key
ladder.why: Sort each word once, then let the hash map do the grouping. One hash lookup per word instead of comparing every pair, at the cost of sorting every word.

ladder.label: 26 wide count vector as the key
ladder.why: The sort is avoidable because only the letter counts matter. A 26 wide tally is a complete signature, so building it is linear in the word length rather than k log k. Requires the word to be lowercase letters only.

hints: What property do two anagrams share that a non-anagram cannot have?
The same multiset of characters. So if you can turn a word into a canonical form, two words are anagrams exactly when their forms match.
Sorting a word makes that canonical form. What could you use as a dictionary key?
The sorted word itself. Group by that key rather than comparing pairs.
Pseudocode: for each word, sort its characters, look that up in a map, and append the original word to the list stored there.

problems.title: Jump Game
problems.statement: You are given an integer array nums. Each element nums[i] represents the maximum jump length available at that position. Start at index 0 and return true if you can reach the last index, or false if it is not possible.
problems.keyIdea: Track the furthest index reachable so far. If the current index passes that frontier, no choice of path could have helped, because the frontier is the best any earlier jump could have bought.

ladder.label: Try every path
ladder.why: Recursively try every jump length from every position. Exponential, because the same suffix is re-explored exponentially many times.

ladder.label: Dynamic programming from the end
ladder.why: Mark every index you can reach, working backwards. Linear time, but it keeps a boolean per index when the answer only ever needs one running number.

ladder.label: Greedy furthest reach
ladder.why: One variable holds the furthest index reachable. If the current index ever passes it, the answer is no. Constant space, single pass, and no array of states.

hints: Do you need to know every reachable position, or just the furthest one?
If you can reach index 9, every index up to 9 is also reachable. Reachability is a prefix, not a scattered set.
Keep a single number: the furthest index anything so far can jump to.
At each index, extend the frontier with i plus nums[i]. If the frontier falls behind the current index, you are stuck.
Pseudocode: reach = 0. For each i, if i > reach return false, else reach = max(reach, i + nums[i]).

problems.title: Merge Intervals
problems.statement: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] equals start i and end i, merge all overlapping intervals and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the input ranges.
problems.keyIdea: Sort by start time, then sweep once. Each interval either extends the run you are building or has to begin a new one, and no interval can ever overlap something more than one position behind.

ladder.label: Repeated pairwise merging until stable
ladder.why: Keep merging any two overlapping intervals until nothing changes. Correct, but it rescans the entire list after every single merge.

ladder.label: Sort by start, then one merge pass
ladder.why: Sorting by start makes every overlap adjacent, so a single left to right pass finishes the job. It still allocates a second n sized array.

ladder.label: In-place merge into the same array
ladder.why: Same sorted sweep, but the result is written back over the input as it goes. The only extra memory is whatever the sort itself needs.

hints: What makes two intervals adjacent in the list rather than scattered?
Sorting. Once intervals are ordered by start, an interval can only overlap the one you are currently building or the one right after it.
Sort by start time, then walk once comparing each start against the current run's end.
If start is at or before the current end, extend the end. Otherwise push a new interval.
Pseudocode: sort by start. For each interval, if it overlaps the last merged one, extend that one's end, else append it.

problems.title: Subsets
problems.statement: Given an integer array nums of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set). The solution must not contain duplicate subsets. Return the subsets in any order.
problems.keyIdea: Record the current path at every node of the search tree, not only at the leaves. Every prefix is itself a valid subset, so the recursion has no base case that stops early.

ladder.label: Enumerate all masks and test each one
ladder.why: Treat the subset as a bitmask, so there are exactly 2 to the n of them and every mask is valid. Thorough and completely ignores the recursive structure that makes this problem teachable.

code.python:
out = []
n = len(nums)
for mask in range(1 << n):
    out.append([nums[i] for i in range(n) if mask & (1 << i)])
return out

ladder.label: Iterative doubling
ladder.why: Start with the empty subset, then for each element add a copy of every subset with that element appended. No recursion, and the doubling structure is visible in the code.

code.python:
out = [[]]
for v in nums:
    out += [sub + [v] for sub in out]
return out

ladder.label: Backtracking, record at every node
ladder.why: Same asymptotics, because you must materialise 2 to the n subsets either way. The win is space: one shared path is mutated in place and copied on the way out, instead of allocating a fresh list per leaf. Recording at entry rather than at the leaf is what makes the empty subset appear without special-casing it.

code.python:
out, path = [], []
def backtrack(start):
    out.append(path[:])
    for i in range(start, len(nums)):
        path.append(nums[i])
        backtrack(i + 1)
        path.pop()
backtrack(0)
return out

hints: How many subsets does a set of n distinct elements have?
Two to the n. Every element is either in or out, and that choice is independent for each one.
In a recursive solution, is a subset only complete at the deepest call?
No. Every partial path is already a valid subset, so record the current path at entry rather than at the exit.
Pseudocode: record a copy of the current path. For each remaining element, add it, recurse from the next index, then remove it.

problems.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
problems.statement: Given an array of integers nums, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence. The sequence elements do not need to appear in any order in nums.
problems.keyIdea: Only start counting from a value that has no predecessor. Doing it that way makes each run visited once, so the total work stays linear even though you appear to walk the whole run for every element.

ladder.label: Sort, then walk runs of adjacent values
ladder.why: Sort first, then a single pass counts consecutive values. Correct and simple, and it ignores the hashing that the problem practically advertises.

code.python:
a = sorted(nums)
best = run = 0
for i, v in enumerate(a):
    run = run + 1 if (i > 0 and v == a[i-1] + 1) else 1
    best = max(best, run)
return best

ladder.label: Walk every run from every element
ladder.why: For each value, walk upward while the successor is present. Looks right, but a long run gets re-walked once per element in it, so the worst case is quadratic on a single dense range.

code.python:
s = set(nums)
best = 0
for v in s:
    length = 1
    while v + length in s:
        length += 1
    best = max(best, length)
return best

ladder.label: Start only at run heads
ladder.why: Add one guard: only walk a run when the current value has no predecessor. Every run is then traversed exactly once, so although you still walk long runs, the total across all values is bounded by n.

hints: Why is walking a run from every single value too slow?
Because a run of length n is walked once from each of its n members, so the work adds up to quadratic.
What distinguishes the first value of a run from every other value in it?
It is the only value in the run whose predecessor is absent. If v minus one is in the set, v is not a run head.
Pseudocode: build a set, then for each v where v minus one is absent, walk upward counting while the successor is present.

problems.title: Two Sum II (Input Array Is Sorted)
problems.statement: Given a 1-indexed array of integers numbers that is already sorted in ascending order and an integer target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target. You may use at most two iterations, and the array must stay unchanged.
problems.keyIdea: The array is already sorted, so the sum is monotone in each cursor: too small means left must move right, too large means right must move left. Each step eliminates a whole side of the remaining space.

ladder.label: Check every pair
ladder.why: Scan the rest of the array for each element. Correct, and it makes no use at all of the sorted property that the problem hands you on purpose.

ladder.label: Binary search for the complement
ladder.why: For each element, binary search for its complement in the remaining range. Better than quadratic, but it still pays a log factor per element when the sorted order allows a linear scan instead.

code.python:
for i, v in enumerate(numbers):
    need = target - v
    lo, hi = i + 1, len(numbers) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if numbers[mid] == need: return [i + 1, mid + 1]
        if numbers[mid] < need: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
return [-1, -1]

ladder.label: Opposing pointers
ladder.why: One pointer from each end. Because the array is sorted, a sum below target rules out every pair that keeps the left value and a smaller right value, so moving left forward discards nothing useful. Each step eliminates one entire side.

code.python:
l, r = 0, len(numbers) - 1
while l < r:
    s = numbers[l] + numbers[r]
    if s == target: return [l + 1, r + 1]
    if s < target: l += 1
    else: r -= 1
return [-1, -1]

hints: What does the sorted order guarantee about the sum as you move one cursor?
The sum is monotone in each direction. Moving left right always increases it, moving right left always decreases it.
If the current sum is too small, which pointer is safe to move?
The left one. Any pair that keeps this left value and pairs it with something smaller than the current right value is even further below target, so none of them work.
Pseudocode: l at the front, r at the back. If the sum is low, move l forward; if high, move r back; equal means done.

problems.title: Number of Islands
problems.statement: Given an m x n 2D binary grid which represents a map of '1's (land) and '0's (waters), return the number of islands. An island is surrounded by water and is formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically. You may assume all four edges of the grid are surrounded by water.
problems.keyIdea: Each new unvisited land cell starts exactly one island. Flood-fill the whole connected component so it is never counted twice.

ladder.label: Repeated flood fill without marking
ladder.why: The fill explores the same component from every starting cell because nothing records that ground was already processed.

ladder.label: Flood fill with visited set
ladder.why: An explicit visited set makes the complexity provably linear, at the cost of auxiliary memory alongside the grid.

ladder.label: Iterative sink as you count
ladder.why: The sink writes its own state, so no auxiliary structure is needed. Same asymptotics as the visited set, but O(1) extra memory.

hints: How do you avoid counting one island twice?
When you find unvisited land, that cell must be the start of a brand new island. Once counted, the whole connected region is finished.
Flood fill from the starting cell, marking every land cell you touch so the outer loop skips it.
Recursive DFS is simplest but can overflow the stack on large grids. An explicit stack keeps memory on the heap.
Pseudocode: on unvisited '1', increment the count, then flood fill all connected '1' cells, marking each as '0' as you visit it.

problems.title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
problems.statement: Implement a trie with insert, search and startsWith. Each node represents a single character and holds links to its children, with a flag marking the end of a word.
problems.keyIdea: A trie stores prefixes as shared path prefixes rather than whole strings. The word 'car' and 'cat' share the nodes for 'c' and 'a', so a prefix query walks the shared path and stops.

ladder.label: Store words in a list and scan
ladder.time: O(n * m) insert, O(n * m) search
ladder.why: Keep every inserted word and check startsWith against each one with string comparison. Correct, and it re-reads the shared prefix on every single lookup, which is exactly the duplication a trie exists to remove.

ladder.label: Nested hash maps
ladder.why: Each node is a dictionary from character to child node, which keeps the shared-prefix structure while avoiding the fixed alphabet array. Lookup is one hash per character.

ladder.label: Fixed alphabet array per node
ladder.why: Same linear behaviour, but a child is a direct array index rather than a hash lookup, so each character costs one bounds check and one load. For a known alphabet that is measurably faster, at the price of allocating 26 slots for nodes that hold far fewer.

hints: What do two words with a common prefix have in common that you could store once?
The path of nodes spelling that prefix. Every word through 'car' shares the same nodes for 'c', 'a' and 'r'.
What does a single trie node need to hold?
Links to its children, and a flag saying whether a word ends exactly here. That flag is what separates a prefix from a complete word.
Pseudocode: for each character, follow or create the child for it, then set a flag marking the final node as a word end.

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
problems.statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the kth largest element in the array. It is not necessarily the kth distinct element.
problems.keyIdea: You only ever need the top k values, so anything outside that set is dead weight. Discarding the rest is what turns a full sort into a partial one.

ladder.label: Sort and index from the end
ladder.why: Sort ascending and read index n minus k. Always correct, but it totally orders every element in order to use k of them.

code.python: return sorted(nums, reverse=True)[k - 1]

ladder.label: Quickselect around a pivot
ladder.why: Partition around a pivot so everything larger goes to one side, then recurse only into the side holding position k. Average linear, but the worst case degenerates to n squared when the pivot keeps landing on an extreme.

code.python:
def quick_select(a, lo, hi, target):
    while lo < hi:
        pivot = a[(lo + hi) // 2]
        i, j = lo, hi
        while i <= j:
            while a[i] < pivot: i += 1
            while a[j] > pivot: j -= 1
            if i <= j:
                a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
                i += 1; j -= 1
        if target <= j: hi = j
        elif target >= i: lo = i
        else: return

a = list(nums)
quick_select(a, 0, len(a) - 1, len(a) - k)
return a[len(a) - k]

ladder.label: Min-heap of size k
ladder.why: Keep only the k largest in a min-heap. The heap top is always the smallest of the current top k, so it is exactly the next value to evict. Cost depends on k, not on n.

code.python:
import heapq

pq = []
for v in nums:
    heapq.heappush(pq, v)
    if len(pq) > k:
        heapq.heappop(pq)
return pq[0]

hints: How many values do you actually need to remember at any moment?
Only k. Every other element is irrelevant the moment you read it.
If you kept the k largest seen so far, what structure answers which one to throw away?
A min-heap of size k. Its top is the smallest of the k largest, so that is the one that gets evicted.
Pseudocode: push each value, and whenever the heap size exceeds k, pop it. The heap top at the end is the answer.

problems.title: Sum of Two Integers
problems.statement: Given two integers a and b, return the sum of the two integers without using the plus or minus operators.
problems.keyIdea: XOR gives the sum without any carry. AND identifies exactly the positions that produce a carry, and shifting that left by one moves the carry into the next position.

ladder.label: Add one bit position at a time
ladder.why: Walk all 32 positions individually, writing the sum bit into the result and shifting the carry up by hand each round. Correct but mechanical, and it always does exactly 32 iterations.

code.python:
result = 0
carry = 0
for i in range(32):
    a_bit = (a >> i) & 1
    b_bit = (b >> i) & 1
    sum_bit = a_bit ^ b_bit ^ carry
    carry = a_bit & b_bit | (a_bit & carry) | (b_bit & carry)
    result |= sum_bit << i
return result

ladder.label: XOR for the sum, AND for the carry
ladder.why: XOR already computes the sum of each bit pair ignoring carries, and AND marks exactly the positions that carry. Shift the carry left and feed it back until it disappears. Usually converges in two or three rounds.

code.python:
MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF

total = (a ^ b) & MASK
carry = ((a & b) << 1) & MASK
while carry:
    total = (total ^ carry) & MASK
    carry = ((total & carry) << 1) & MASK

return total - (1 << 32) if total >> 31 else total

ladder.label: Branchless fixed-width carry propagation
ladder.why: Identical arithmetic, but the loop always runs 32 times with no data dependent exit. On a fixed width word the answer is identical while the branch becomes fully predictable, which is what you want in hot code.

code.python:
MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF

total = (a ^ b) & MASK
carry = (a & b) & MASK
for _ in range(32):
    total, carry = (total ^ carry) & MASK, ((total & carry) << 1) & MASK

return total - (1 << 32) if total >> 31 else total

hints: Which bitwise operator gives you 1 only where exactly one input bit is 1?
XOR. That is the sum of a bit pair when you ignore carrying entirely.
Which operator identifies the positions where a carry will actually be produced?
AND, shifted one place left. That carry then has to be added back into the sum, which means feeding it through the same XOR step again.
Pseudocode: sum = a XOR b, carry = a AND b. While carry is nonzero: next = (sum AND carry) shifted left, sum = sum XOR carry, carry = next.

problems.title: Koko Eating Bananas
problems.statement: Koko can eat a pile of bananas in one hour if the pile has at most x bananas. She can choose any eating speed x, and eats at the same rate. Given piles, find the minimum x such that Koko can finish all piles within h hours.
problems.keyIdea: The predicate 'can Koko finish at speed x' is monotonic: if she can finish at speed x, she can finish at any higher speed. So binary search over the answer space, not over the piles.

ladder.label: Try every speed from 1 upward
ladder.why: Test each candidate speed and take the first that works. Linear in the maximum pile, which for large piles means testing hundreds of thousands of speeds one at a time.

ladder.label: Binary search the answer with a separate predicate
ladder.why: Extract the feasibility test into its own function and binary search the smallest speed that passes. The monotonicity guarantees no passing speed is skipped, because speed up the pile times only ever decrease.

code.python:
def can_finish(speed):
    hours = 0
    for p in piles:
        hours += (p + speed - 1) // speed
        if hours > h: return False
    return True

lo, hi = 1, max(piles)
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if can_finish(mid): hi = mid
    else: lo = mid + 1
return lo

ladder.label: Binary search with early exit in the predicate
ladder.why: Same asymptotics, but the predicate bails out the moment accumulated hours exceed the budget. On a failing candidate that often saves most of the scan, and because the predicate is checked more often than the binary search steps, that saving dominates in practice.

code.python:
lo, hi = 1, max(piles)
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    hours = 0
    for p in piles:
        hours += (p + mid - 1) // mid
        if hours > h: break
    else:
        hi = mid
        continue
    lo = mid + 1
return lo

hints: If Koko can finish at speed x, what can she say about speed x plus one?
She can certainly finish at x plus one too. Faster speed never increases the hours needed, so the predicate is monotonic.
What does a monotonic predicate over a numeric range invite?
A binary search for the smallest value that passes. You are searching the answer, not the data.
Pseudocode: lo starts at 1, hi at the largest pile. Take the midpoint, test feasibility, and on success move hi down to it, otherwise move lo up past it.

problems.title: Sort an Array
problems.statement: Given an integer array nums, return it sorted in ascending order. You must solve the problem without using any built-in sorting function.
problems.keyIdea: Quicksort picks a pivot and partitions so that everything on one side is smaller than the pivot. The partition is the actual insight: once values land on the correct side you never have to look at them again.

ladder.label: Selection sort
ladder.why: Repeatedly find the smallest remaining value and swap it into place. Every comparison is used, which makes it instructive, and there are n squared of them regardless of the input, which makes it unusable.

code.python:
a = list(nums)
for i in range(len(a)):
    lo = min(range(i, len(a)), key=lambda k: a[k])
    a[i], a[lo] = a[lo], a[i]
return a

ladder.label: Merge sort
ladder.why: Halve the array, sort each half, merge them in one linear pass. Guaranteed n log n on every input and stable, at the cost of an auxiliary buffer.

code.python:
a = list(nums)
def msort(lo, hi):
    if lo >= hi: return
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    msort(lo, mid); msort(mid + 1, hi)
    i, j, k = lo, mid + 1, lo
    while i <= mid and j <= hi:
        if a[i] <= a[j]: a[k] = a[i]; i += 1
        else: a[k] = a[j]; j += 1
        k += 1
    while i <= mid: a[k] = a[i]; i += 1; k += 1
    while j <= hi: a[k] = a[j]; j += 1; k += 1
msort(0, len(a) - 1)
return a

ladder.label: Quicksort with median-of-three pivot
ladder.why: Partition around a pivot chosen as the median of first, middle and last. That single change is what stops the sorted input case, which is exactly the input that makes a naive pivot quadratic. No auxiliary buffer, and the sort happens in place.

hints: What is the one comparison pattern that appears in every n squared sort?
It keeps comparing pairs that cannot both be the answer. Selection sort compares everything against the current minimum even after the minimum is already known.
If you split the array in half and solve both halves, how do you get the whole thing back in order?
Merge them. Both halves are sorted, so one linear pass interleaves them.
Pseudocode for the merge: compare the front elements of both halves, take the smaller, repeat until one half is empty, then append the rest.

problems.title: Merge k Sorted Lists
problems.statement: You are given an array of k linked lists, each sorted in ascending order. Merge all the lists into one sorted linked list and return it.
problems.keyIdea: The next smallest element can only be the head of one of the remaining lists, which is exactly the extreme element a heap maintains. Pushing one node per list keeps the heap size at k rather than growing with total input.

ladder.label: Merge pairwise until one list remains
ladder.why: Merge two lists at a time, repeatedly, until one remains. The asymptotics are acceptable, but you walk most of the data more than once across the log k rounds.

code.python:
merged = lists[0]
for nxt in lists[1:]:
    merged = merge_two(merged, nxt)
return merged

def merge_two(a, b):
    dummy = ListNode(0); tail = dummy
    while a and b:
        if a.val <= b.val: tail.next = a; a = a.next
        else: tail.next = b; b = b.next
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = a if a else b
    return dummy.next

ladder.label: Concatenate then sort
ladder.why: Flatten everything into one array and sort it. It discards the fact that every input was already sorted, which is the entire reason a better solution exists, and it costs n log n rather than n log k.

ladder.label: Min-heap seeded with one head per list
ladder.why: The heap holds at most k elements, one per list, so the cost of each extraction is log k rather than log N. That is the whole reason to use a heap here, and it also drops the extra memory the pairwise merge needs.

code.python:
import heapq

heap = [(node.val, i, node) for i, node in enumerate(lists) if node]
heapq.heapify(heap)

dummy = ListNode(0); tail = dummy
while heap:
    _, i, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
    tail.next = node
    tail = tail.next
    if node.next:
        heapq.heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))
return dummy.next

hints: The smallest remaining value can only be at the head of one of the lists. How many candidates are there at any moment?
At most k, one per list still being merged. You only ever need to compare those k candidates.
What data structure repeatedly extracts the smallest of a small dynamic set?
A min-heap. Seed it with one head per list and push each node's successor as you take it, so the heap never grows past k.
Pseudocode: push every non-null head. Pop the smallest, append it, and push its next if it has one. Repeat until the heap is empty.

problems.title: Minimum Window Substring
problems.statement: Given two strings s and t, return the minimum window in s that will contain all the characters in t, including duplicates, or the empty string if no such window exists.
problems.keyIdea: You need counts, not set membership, because t has duplicates. Track how many distinct characters are still missing and shrink from the left while that count is zero, recording the tightest window each time it becomes valid.

ladder.label: Every window with a count check
ladder.why: For each start index, extend the window and count characters. Clearly correct, and it rescans the same characters once per starting position.

code.cpp:
// For each start, extend until the window covers t, then break.
// Worst case every character is visited once per start position.

ladder.label: Sliding window with a satisfied counter
ladder.why: One pass with two cursors. Instead of comparing whole maps on every move, keep a single count of how many distinct characters are still missing, so each step is an integer compare rather than a set containment check.

code.python:
if len(t) > len(s): return ''
need = [0] * 128
for c in t: need[ord(c)] += 1
required = sum(1 for v in need if v)
missing = required
have = [0] * 128

best, best_start, left = len(s) + 1, 0, 0
for right, c in enumerate(s):
    o = ord(c)
    if need[o] > 0:
        have[o] += 1
        if have[o] == need[o]: missing -= 1
    while missing == 0:
        if right - left + 1 < best:
            best, best_start = right - left + 1, left
        o = ord(s[left]); left += 1
        if need[o] > 0:
            have[o] -= 1
            if have[o] < need[o]: missing += 1
return s[best_start:best_start + best] if best <= len(s) else ''

ladder.label: Sliding window with a last-seen index array
ladder.why: Same asymptotics as the counter version, but it drops the inner while loop entirely: the left edge jumps straight to one past the last seen position of the rarest outstanding character. That removes the repeated left-advance work, which is the only quadratic risk in the counter form on adversarial input.

code.python:
if len(t) > len(s): return ''
need = [0] * 128
for c in t: need[ord(c)] += 1
required = sum(1 for v in need if v)

last_seen = [-1] * 128
seen = 0
best, best_start, left = len(s) + 1, 0, 0
for right, c in enumerate(s):
    o = ord(c)
    if need[o] > 0:
        last_seen[o] = right
        seen += 1
    while seen == required:
        if right - left + 1 < best:
            best, best_start = right - left + 1, left
        p = ord(s[left]); left += 1
        if need[p] > 0 and last_seen[p] < left:
            seen -= 1
return s[best_start:best_start + best] if best <= len(s) else ''
code.cpp:
// Track lastSeen[c] for each required character; advance left past a
// character whose last occurrence has already fallen out of the window.

hints: Does t contain duplicate characters?
Yes, and that changes the data structure. A set of seen characters is not enough, because 'aab' is not satisfied by one a.
What single number tells you whether the current window is valid?
How many distinct required characters are still missing. It hits zero exactly when the window covers t.
Pseudocode: extend right one character at a time, decrementing missing when a requirement is newly met. While missing is zero, record the length and advance left.

problems.title: Range Sum Query - Mutable
problems.statement: Given an array nums, answer queries of the form: what is the sum of the values in nums[index1] to nums[index2], inclusive? Support updates where nums[index] is set to a new value, and queries, efficiently.
problems.keyIdea: A prefix-sum array makes queries instant but every update a full rebuild. A Fenwick tree keeps prefix sums under both operations in logarithmic time by storing partial sums over ranges of power-of-two length, which is what the lowbit walk indexes.

ladder.label: Rebuild a prefix array on every update
ladder.why: Keep a prefix sum array so a query is one subtraction. The moment a value changes you must recompute every prefix after it, which turns each update into a linear pass.

ladder.label: Segment tree
ladder.time: O(log n) query, O(log n) update
ladder.why: Store the sum over each interval of a binary partition of the array. Query and update both descend only one root-to-leaf path, so both are logarithmic. The combine is associative, which is the requirement that makes a segment tree possible at all.

ladder.label: Fenwick tree over partial sums
ladder.time: O(log n) query, O(log n) update
ladder.why: Same asymptotics as a segment tree with a quarter of the memory, because it exploits a property sums specifically have: prefix sums are invertible, so one flat array of partial sums over power-of-two ranges is enough. The lowbit walk makes each step jump over exactly the block it accounts for.

hints: What does a prefix sum array give you for free, and what does it cost on an update?
Queries are one subtraction. The problem is that changing one value invalidates every prefix after it.
If prefix sums are invertible, do you need a full tree?
No. A Fenwick tree is a single flat array where each slot holds the sum over a range whose length is its own lowest set bit.
Pseudocode for the Fenwick: to add at a one based index, walk forward by i AND minus i. To get a prefix sum, walk backward the same way. A range is the difference of two prefixes.
